column3: A Jenga tower in real 3D. A tall tower of wooden blocks in perspective (three per layer, alternating direction, shaded faces, wood seams), slowly rotating. The time is the gaps: the blocks that have been pulled out leave holes whose pattern, seen face-on on the big front faces of the tower, forms the numerals; or the pulled blocks are stacked on top as the digits. Design the face so a stranger reads the time clearly. Always alive: the tower sways a little, an unseen finger taps a block that wiggles, the camera orbits. Minute turn: a block is pushed out with a slow nudge and teeters, then is placed on top; the time's pattern changes. Hour: the tower topples in a 3D crash and is restacked.

An IBM Selectric typewriter's golf-ball type element in real 3D, big in the frame: a sphere covered in rows of raised characters, spinning and tilting at high speed to select each character and striking the paper with a snap, the ribbon lifting. The time is typed: the paper beside or below shows the typed time in a crisp typewriter face, and the ball always moves. Design both the raised characters on the ball (foreshortened in 3D) and the typed letterforms. Always alive: the ball hovers, the carriage drifts, the ribbon shimmers. Minute turn: the carriage returns, the line feeds, the ball whirls and types the new minute, character by character. Hour: a rapid flourish, a bell ding, the page is pulled out and a fresh sheet rolled in.

A PEZ candy dispenser in real 3D: a character head on a hinged lid tips back to reveal a candy brick, the stem holding a stack of bricks. The minutes are printed on the candy bricks (bold numerals on the end of each brick); the hour is the character's identity or a number on its stem. Design a cute but bold character head that reads at 1x. Always alive: the dispenser sways and rotates, the head bobs, the spring inside creeps. Minute turn: the head tips back, the top brick with the old minute shoots out and tumbles away, the stack springs up and the next brick (the new minute) rises into place, the head snaps shut. Hour: the dispenser is refilled with a whole new stack, sliding in from below.

A Newton's cradle in real 3D: five chrome balls hanging on V-shaped wires from a frame, swinging and clicking, with specular highlights and reflections of each other. The numerals are engraved or carried on the balls (big bold numerals on the end balls, or the balls swing out to show the time). Make the swing physical (the momentum transfer, the small middle jiggle). Always alive: the cradle clicks steadily; the camera orbits slowly. Minute turn: a hand stops the balls, swaps the end ball with the new minute, and lets it swing. Hour: all balls lifted and released together, a chaotic dance that settles.

Paper cutting: a pair of scissors in real 3D snips the numerals out of a sheet of paper. The paper is a lit sheet with a slight curl; the cut-out numerals lift and curl at their edges, casting shadows, while the scrap peels away. Make the scissors' blades open and close with each cut, and follow a path. Always alive: the paper flutters, offcuts drift, the scissors snip in the air. Minute turn: the old numeral is crumpled and tossed away, and the scissors cut the new one from the sheet, snip by snip along its outline. Hour: a whole chain of paper figures is cut and unfolded across the screen.

A kid in profile chewing bubblegum, drawn bold and characterful at 1x (cap, cheeks, big eyes). The minute is a gum bubble: the kid blows a big round bubble (a glossy sphere with a crisp highlight and a slight wobble) with the numeral printed on it, inflating and deflating as the kid breathes. The hour is on the kid's cap or on a gumball machine behind. Always alive: chewing, the bubble breathes and wobbles, the kid's eyes cross at the bubble. Minute turn: the bubble grows too big and POPS, gum splatters over the face, the kid peels it off, chews and blows the new minute bubble. Hour: a giant bubble lifts the kid off the ground and floats away, then pops and drops them back.
